steps.title: Proposing, objecting, supporting
steps.html:
Proposing with an infinitive. The frames built on would be are completed by to + verb: One alternative would be to install…, A better way forward would be to fit…, The simplest option would be to move it. These are the most formal of the set and the most common in writing.

Proposing with -ing. Worth is always followed by -ing: Would it be worth putting in fake cameras? So are the frames with the preposition in: any point in changing…, no harm in trying…. And suggest keeps its pattern from lesson 33: I would suggest fitting….

Proposing with a clause. What if we paint the walls? treats the idea as a real possibility; What if we painted the walls? is one step more tentative, and is the safer form in a meeting where you are not in charge. How about and What about take -ing: How about painting the walls?

Objecting. English objects with a reason attached: I do not think that is an option, because…, I am not convinced by those, We need to take cost into consideration. A bare no ends a discussion that the speaker usually wants to continue.

Supporting and deciding. That would be an effective solution, There is no harm in doing that as well, Let us do that; I will look into it. A proposal without somebody named to act on it is a conversation, not a decision.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• Would it be worth to put in cameras?
  • Is there any point to change the lock?
  • There is no harm to try it.
  • One alternative would be installing cameras — possible, but the infinitive is standard here.
  • What if we to paint the walls? or What about paint the walls?

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
What to do about vandalism at a small site

Start with a definition, because vandalism and theft need different answers. If nothing has been taken, you are dealing with damage for its own sake, usually late at night, usually in the one corner nobody can see from the road. Before proposing anything, analyse the pattern: two incidents this month, both after eleven, both in the unlit corner, and the gate lock untouched, which tells you access was over the wall.

The obvious answer is a security camera, and for most small sites it is the wrong one. Cameras are expensive to install, difficult to maintain, and incapable of stopping anything by themselves; somebody still has to watch the recording and act on it. Fake cameras are cheaper and not quite useless, but anybody who has looked at one twice is not convinced. A better way forward would be to fit movement-sensor lights: a well-lit corner is a poor place to spend twenty minutes with a spray can, and two of your own staff are probably capable of fitting them in an afternoon.

There is no harm in adding one cheap precaution as well — anti-climb paint on the wall they came over, for instance. Is there any point in changing a lock that was never broken? None, and money spent there is money not spent on the lights.

The mistake most people make is treating this as a purchase rather than an experiment. Fix a review date, write down what you expect to happen, and be precise about what you are measuring. If the incidents stop, you have your answer. If they move to another corner, you have learned something worth more than the lights cost.
